header.toolkit_paper_citation: Simon Huband, Luigi Barone, Lyndon While, Phil Hingston, "A Scalable Multi-objective Test Problem Toolkit," Evolutionary Multi-Criterion Optimization: Third International Conference, EMO 2005, LNCS 3410, pp. 280-295, Springer-Verlag, 2005 ("corrected version: 22 June 2005").
header.toolkit_license_note: repo-root LICENSE (GPLv2) covers richardeverson's own Python wrapper only; every file under WFG_v2006.03.28/ carries the WFG authors' own permissive academic notice instead (T5/T6 module doc, quoted in full). ORACLE-ONLY use: no toolkit C++ line enters this repository.
header.probe_compile_command: g++ -std=c++11 -O2 -o probe probe.cpp WFG_v2006.03.28/Toolkit/*.cpp -- probe.cpp is a scratchpad-only CLI driver (T5/T6, extended by T7 verification: re-verified this task by recompiling from the existing probe.cpp source into a byte-identical binary, `diff`-checked bit-for-bit against WFG1 and WFG9 probe outputs before use) calling only the toolkit's own unmodified public headers (ExampleProblems.h/TransFunctions.h/ShapeFunctions.h); invocation: `probe wfgN k M z1 z2 ... zn`, stdout `%.17g`-precision (std::setprecision(17)) space-separated objective values.
header.pymoo_install: uv venv <scratchpad>/pymoo-venv (T4 precedent, reused unmodified this task) then VIRTUAL_ENV=<scratchpad>/pymoo-venv uv pip install pymoo -- PyPI, scratchpad-only. Version re-verified this task via `python -c "import pymoo; print(pymoo.__version__)"`.
header.pymoo_scaling_convention_finding: ESTABLISHED FROM SOURCE (not assumed): pymoo.problems.many.wfg.WFG.__init__ sets `xl=0.0, xu=2*np.arange(1,n_var+1)` -- the SAME native [0, 2i] per-coordinate domain the toolkit and sezgi use (the paper's own zi,max=2i, Table 6), NOT an internally-exposed [0,1]-normalized interface; pymoo normalizes internally (`y = x / self.xu`, wfg.py line ~198/264/304/etc.) but its PUBLIC evaluate() takes the same raw z domain as the toolkit's probe and this fixture's `x` values -- confirmed empirically, not merely by reading the source: `WFG1(n_var=8,n_obj=2,k=4,l=4).evaluate([[0]*8])` == [1.0, 5.0] and `.evaluate([[2,4,...,16]])` == [3.0, 1.0], bit-identical to the compiled toolkit's own `probe wfg1 4 2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0` / `probe wfg1 4 2 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16` output and to wfg.rs's own `wfg1_matches_toolkit_all_configs` unit-test literals for the same two points. No scaling mismatch: every x below is passed to pymoo's evaluate() UNCHANGED from the same value passed to the toolkit probe and to sezgi's Wfg.
header.tolerance_rationale: 1e-8 relative: independent summation order across sezgi (Rust), the compiled toolkit (C++), and pymoo (numpy) means bit-exactness is not expected from any of these pairings -- same value and same rationale cec2014_reference_values.json's/cec2022_reference_values.json's own headers use (M3-3 T8 / M3-6 T5 precedent, mirrored here). In practice this task's own generation run measured far tighter: max relative delta 2.8095583961488147e-15 between the compiled toolkit and pymoo over all 288 individual objective-value comparisons (108 probe points x up to 3 objectives each) -- near f64 machine epsilon, i.e. NO divergence class was found or needed for this task's coverage (see divergence_classes_note below).
header.divergence_classes_note: EMPTY, not merely unpopulated: pymoo's WFG1-WFG9 (pymoo.problems.many.wfg, read in full this task) is source-verified to implement the SAME EMO2005/toolkit transition-stack formulas as sezgi's own wfg.rs (Table 6 t1..t4 per problem, same shape/transformation-function definitions, same S/A constants, same native [0,2i] domain -- see pymoo_scaling_convention_finding above) -- unlike opfunu's CEC2014/CEC2022 hybrids/compositions (cec2014_reference_values.json's own divergence_classes map), no shuffle-before-rotate, missing-shift, or wrong-submatrix class of bug was found in pymoo's WFG module for this fixture's coverage (1..=9 x {(m=2,k=4,l=4),(m=3,k=4,l=4),(m=3,k=6,l=20)} x {zero,max,generic,random} = 108 probe points, 288 individual objective-value comparisons): every comparison measured at most 2.8095583961488147e-15 relative deviation, far under the 1e-8 tolerance -- consistent with floating-point summation- order noise between numpy (pymoo) and the toolkit's own C++ loop order, not an algorithmic disagreement. `points[*][*].exclude` is `null` for every point in this fixture (no exclusion tag is used anywhere) precisely because no divergence needed one; the field is retained (not dropped) so a FUTURE re-generation that DOES find a pymoo divergence (e.g. if this fixture's coverage is later widened to m>3 or to WFG variants pymoo's own module docs do not exercise) can tag it the same way cec2014_reference_values.json already does, without a schema change.
header.coverage: which in 1..=9 (WFG1-WFG9, the full suite) x (m,k,l) in {(2,4,4),(3,4,4),(3,6,20)} = 27 combinations x 4 probe points each = 108 total probe points. All 27 (which,m,k,l) combinations satisfy every constructor constraint checked by BOTH sezgi's own Wfg::new (k % (m-1) == 0 and k>0; l>0, additionally even for WFG2/WFG3) and pymoo's own WFG.validate (same k%(m-1)==0 check, PLUS pymoo's own stricter k>=4 minimum, PLUS WFG2/WFG3's l%2==0) -- verified programmatically before generation (this script would have raised on `Wfg2(...)`/pymoo `WFG.__init__` otherwise); no combo needed substitution.
header.domain: TRUE (not internally-normalized) domain: x_i in [0, 2i] for i=1..n (n=k+l), the paper's own zi,max=2i (Table 6), matching sezgi's own Wfg::new domain and the toolkit probe's own raw z-vector CLI argument convention (see pymoo_scaling_convention_finding above for pymoo's identical public convention).

probe_points.zero: all-zeros, length n=k+l -- the lower domain boundary.
probe_points.max: z_i = 2*i for i=1..n -- the upper domain boundary (zi,max, Table 6).
probe_points.generic: z_i = PATTERN[(i-1) mod 8] * 2*i, PATTERN = [0.1, 0.9, 0.35, 0.6, 0.25, 0.75, 0.5, 0.15] -- the SAME deterministic period-8 fraction pattern, computed with the SAME f64 arithmetic order, as wfg.rs's own `generic_z` test helper (T5/T6's own fixture-transcription-hazard fix, module doc: hand-rounding this pattern's decimal literals was found to produce ~5.6% relative error via b_poly's alpha=0.02 exponent amplifying sub-ULP differences -- this fixture avoids the hazard the same way T5/T6 did, by generating the value in code, never hand-transcribing a rounded literal).
probe_points.random: python3 random.Random(20060328 + which*100000 + m*1000 + k*10 + l).uniform(0, 2*i) drawn once per coordinate i=1..n in ascending order -- one independent seeded draw per (which,m,k,l) combination, fully reproducible (gen_fixture.py in this task's report). Base constant 20060328 is the toolkit's own release-version date (WFG_v2006.03.28), mirroring cec2014_reference_values.json's own report-year-styled seed-base convention (20140101). Absolute domain point (not an offset), range [0, 2i] -- the paper's own per-coordinate domain, not a narrower or rescaled interior subset.

header.generation_procedure: For each of the 27 (which,m,k,l) combinations, 4 points (zero, max, generic, random, defined above) were evaluated against BOTH the compiled toolkit probe (subprocess, argv floats passed via Python repr() for full round-trip precision, stdout parsed at std::setprecision(17)) and pymoo's WFG{which}(n_var=k+l, n_obj=m, k=k, l=l).evaluate([[x]], return_values_of=['F']) -- same x array, no rescaling (see pymoo_scaling_convention_finding). Every stored value is either a freshly-computed Python float (the z-vector coordinates) or a float() parse of the probe's own stdout token -- never a hand-rounded decimal literal (the T5/T6 fixture-transcription-hazard lesson, this fixture's own `probe_points.generic` note). json.dump(..., indent=2) serializes every float via Python's shortest-round-trip repr, which is bit-faithful to the underlying f64 (same convention cec2014_reference_values.json already uses).
